questions.q: Why does this lesson argue for building a standing portfolio rather than leaving case-study work in scratch documents from each lesson?
options: Because scratch documents are technically impossible to save
Because without deliberately collecting the work, the real thinking produced in each case study gets done once and then effectively thrown away
Because portfolios are a mandatory requirement for completing this course
Because scratch documents cannot contain diagrams
questions.explain: The core argument is about reuse — a portfolio preserves and organizes work that would otherwise be lost once a given lesson's scratch document is abandoned.

questions.q: What does a useful portfolio entry per case study focus on capturing, according to this lesson?
options: A verbatim transcript of the original scenario text
Every quiz question ever answered about that case study
A complete recording of every mock-session Q&A exchange
A compact summary of the reasoning: key constraints, stated assumptions with consequences, top risks and their answers, compact blueprint bullets, and the best rejected-alternatives entries
questions.explain: The entry is meant to be a summary of the reasoning, reviewable in a few minutes — not a re-creation of the original scenario or a transcript of every exercise done about it.

questions.q: What test does this lesson reuse from Lesson 9 to decide what to cut from a portfolio entry?
options: The cost-benefit test
The likelihood-and-impact test
The removal test — if cutting a piece of content wouldn't change how useful the entry is under future time pressure, cut it
The segregation-of-duties test
questions.explain: The same removal test used to separate implied constraints from decorative detail is reapplied here to decide what belongs in a compact, reusable portfolio entry.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend organizing portfolio entries with domain tags (data, security, integration, identity, delivery), not just by company name?
options: Because a specific decision needs to be findable by the domain a new question is actually about, supporting fast retrieval under time pressure
Because domain tags are required by Salesforce's certification program
Because company names cannot be used as organizing labels in any system
Because domain tags replace the need for a scenario summary entirely
questions.explain: The organizing priority is retrieval speed — tagging by domain lets you find relevant past reasoning quickly when a new question is about a specific domain, not just a specific company.

questions.q: What is the fastest recommended way to build a first real portfolio entry, according to this lesson?
options: Invent a brand-new scenario specifically for the portfolio
Wait until after completing the entire course before starting any portfolio work
Copy another student's portfolio entry and adapt it
Compress the case study you already know best (likely the one used in an earlier mock session) down to this lesson's compact format
questions.explain: The course has already generated seven case studies' worth of reasoning across earlier labs — the fastest path to a first entry is compressing existing work, not starting from a new scenario.
